name: A01: Broken Access Control
evidence: Multiple authenticated, resource-scoped routes with ID parameters exist (e.g., GET /api/Users/:id, GET /api/Cards/:id, DELETE /api/Addresss/:id) and use auth middleware like security.isAuthorized(), security.appendUserId(), or security.denyAll(). However, inconsistent enforcement is evident: e.g., /api/Recycles/:id has auth: null + middleware: ["recycles.getRecycleItem()"] — no authorization check — and /api/SecurityAnswers/:id uses security.denyAll() but is also exposed via auto-CRUD ALL methods. This structural pattern of ID-based resource access with mixed/missing auth enforcement satisfies the structural prerequisite.

name: A02: Cryptographic Failures
evidence: Explicit use of JWT (jsonwebtoken v0.4.0), TOTP (twoFactorAuth.setup/verify), password handling (login, reset-password, change-password endpoints), and encryption keys served via /encryptionkeys/:file route. Dependencies include jsonwebtoken, @types/jsonwebtoken, and crypto-related tooling (test/files/encrypt.py, decrypt.py). Passwords are excluded from auto-CRUD responses (excludeAttributes: ["password","totpSecret"]), indicating awareness — but presence of crypto operations and key exposure surface confirms structural prerequisites.

name: A03: Injection
evidence: Multiple high-risk parsers present: js-yaml (v3.14.0) used in /file-upload handler for YAML parsing; libxml2-wasm for XML parsing (handleXmlUpload); and raw SQL/NoSQL implied by Sequelize ORM usage with models including User, Product, Feedback, etc. Additionally, auto-CRUD routes (e.g., /api/Users) accept arbitrary query params (pagination, filtering) without visible sanitization in route definitions — a known injection vector when ORM query builders are misused. No evidence of parameterized queries or input validation in route metadata.

name: A04: Insecure Design
evidence: Insecure design requires analysis of threat modeling, business logic flaws, and architectural decisions (e.g., flawed workflows, missing defense-in-depth layers). While architecture shows features enabling abuse (e.g., undocumented /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress, /b2b/v2/orders, Easter eggs, paywall endpoints), it lacks explicit evidence of *inherently flawed design patterns* (e.g., race conditions, flawed cryptographic protocols, or intentional bypass logic). Absence of threat-model.json content or design spec prevents definitive judgment.

name: A05: Security Misconfiguration
evidence: Multiple misconfiguration indicators: permissive file serving (/ftp, /.well-known, /encryptionkeys, /support/logs) with directory listing enabled (serveIndexMiddleware + { icons: true, view: 'details' }); lack of security headers (helmet v4.6.0 is present but no evidence of configuration — e.g., no CSP, HSTS, or XSS protection settings shown); XML parser (libxml2-wasm) with no indication of entity expansion disabled; and exposure of sensitive files (security.txt, csaf, logs, keys) without authentication or IP restriction on many paths.

name: A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
evidence: Dependency list includes known vulnerable versions: jsonwebtoken v0.4.0 (severe CVE-2018-1000866, CVE-2020-28032), js-yaml v3.14.0 (CVE-2022-29078, CVE-2023-28775), multer v1.4.5-lts.1 (CVE-2022-24435), and express-jwt v0.1.3 (obsolete, unmaintained, multiple auth bypass CVEs). Version pins are present and outdated — satisfying structural prerequisite for component vulnerability exposure.

name: A07: Identification and Authentication Failures
evidence: Full auth lifecycle implemented: login (/rest/user/login), password reset (/rest/user/reset-password with rate limiting), 2FA setup/verify/disable (/rest/2fa/*), TOTP, session management, and credential recovery flows. However, critical weaknesses are structurally evident: /rest/user/reset-password has no auth requirement and is rate-limited only at the route level (not tied to user identity), and /api/Users POST allows registration without CAPTCHA or bot mitigation beyond client-side checks. Auth infrastructure exists — and is demonstrably incomplete — fulfilling the prerequisite.

name: A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures
evidence: Webhook handling (lib/webhook.ts), plugin-like dynamic loading (routes/*.ts imported dynamically), deserialization surfaces (YAML upload via js-yaml, XML via libxml2-wasm, JSON in API bodies), and integrity-critical features (data export, wallet balance updates, order checkout) all rely on untrusted input. Auto-CRUD routes accept arbitrary payloads (e.g., POST /api/Users) with no schema validation visible in route definition. The presence of deserializers and unvalidated object construction satisfies structural prerequisites.

name: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
evidence: Explicit logging infrastructure present: metrics.observeFileUploadMetricsMiddleware(), metrics.serveMetrics(), audit.json log file, and dedicated /support/logs endpoint serving log files. However, no evidence of intrusion detection, anomaly correlation, or alerting — only passive collection and exposure. Presence of logging modules (lib/logger.ts, metrics, audit.json) and log-serving routes confirms structural prerequisite for monitoring failures.

name: A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
evidence: Multiple endpoints accept and process external URLs: /profile/image/url (handler: profileImageUrlUpload), /rest/track-order/:id (implies external carrier integration), /rest/country-mapping (likely fetches remote geolocation data), and /rest/web3/* endpoints (interact with Ethereum nodes). No SSRF mitigation (e.g., allowlists, URL parsing/validation, network restrictions) is indicated in route middleware or dependency list. Structural prerequisite — outbound HTTP calls with dynamic user-controlled input — is satisfied.

name: API1: Broken Object Level Authorization
evidence: Direct object references (DOR) via :id path params are pervasive across REST API surface (e.g., /api/Users/:id, /api/Cards/:id, /api/Addresss/:id) and auto-CRUD routes. Authorization is inconsistently applied: some routes enforce security.isAuthorized(), others use security.denyAll(), and several (e.g., /api/Recycles/:id, /api/Hints/:id) have auth: null. This matches the canonical BOLA pattern — ID-based access without per-object ownership checks — confirmed by route structure and auth metadata.

name: API2: Broken Authentication
evidence: Authentication mechanisms exist (JWT, TOTP, session tokens), but structural flaws are evident: /rest/user/reset-password accepts unauthenticated POST with no binding to user context; /api/Users POST allows admin registration bypass (verify.registerAdminChallenge is a challenge, not a guard); and /rest/2fa/setup lacks pre-authentication binding. These are API-specific auth failures — distinct from A07 — and directly observable in route auth/middleware configuration.

name: API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorization
evidence: Auto-CRUD routes (e.g., /api/Users) expose full model attributes except explicitly excluded ones (excludeAttributes: ["password","totpSecret"]). However, other models (Product, Feedback, Complaint) have no exclusions — meaning PATCH/PUT requests could overwrite sensitive fields (e.g., isAdmin, isDeleted, status) without field-level authorization. Route definitions show no property-level access control logic — only full-object CRUD — satisfying the structural prerequisite.

name: API4: Unrestricted Resource Consumption
evidence: Rate limiting is applied selectively (e.g., /rest/2fa/*, /rest/user/reset-password, /rest/basket) but absent on high-resource endpoints: file uploads (/file-upload, /profile/image/file), search (/rest/products/search), metrics (/metrics), and auto-CRUD bulk operations (e.g., GET /api/Users with pagination). No global rate limiting or request-size caps (e.g., body-parser limits) are declared in route config — satisfying structural prerequisite for DoS/resource exhaustion vectors.

name: API5: Broken Function Level Authorization
evidence: Function-level endpoints exist with inconsistent auth: /api/Products/:id DELETE uses security.denyAll(), while /api/Products POST uses security.isAuthorized(); /api/Challenges POST uses security.denyAll(), yet /api/Challenges/:id is auto-CRUD ALL — exposing read/update/delete to unprivileged users. Critical admin functions (e.g., /api/Quantitys/:id DELETE, /api/PrivacyRequests GET) are either unauthenticated or denyAll — indicating missing role-based function gating. Structural prerequisite confirmed.

name: API6: Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows
evidence: Business-critical flows lack authorization: /rest/basket/:id/checkout (payment) has auth: null; /rest/user/data-export (GDPR export) requires only security.appendUserId() — no consent or scope validation; /rest/web3/walletExploitAddress accepts arbitrary payloads; and /b2b/v2/orders is protected only by security.isAuthorized() — no tenant isolation or B2B-specific auth. These are sensitive workflows exposed without contextual authorization — structural prerequisite met.

name: API7: Server Side Request Forgery
evidence: Same SSRF surfaces as A10, but API-specific: /profile/image/url (arbitrary URL fetch), /rest/track-order/:id (likely resolves carrier URLs), and /rest/web3/* endpoints (connect to Ethereum RPC endpoints). All are REST API endpoints accepting untrusted URLs — satisfying API7’s structural definition.

name: API8: Security Misconfiguration
evidence: API-specific misconfigurations: Swagger docs cover only 1 of 137+ API paths (massive documentation gap); /metrics endpoint exposed unauthenticated; /support/logs serves raw logs publicly; /encryptionkeys exposes keys without auth; and auto-CRUD routes lack input validation or output sanitization. These are API surface misconfigurations — distinct from A05 — confirmed by route metadata.

name: API9: Improper Inventory Management
evidence: Swagger documents only 1 path; 109 hand-written and 28 auto-CRUD API routes are undocumented. Undocumented surfaces (e.g., /rest/memories, /rest/chat, /rest/web3/*, /b2b/v2/orders) create shadow APIs — classic inventory failure. File inventory shows extensive unclassified TypeScript/JSON assets, further indicating poor API asset tracking.

name: API10: Unsafe Consumption of APIs
evidence: No evidence of third-party API consumption in route definitions, dependencies, or LLM tooling (tools use local DB/Sequelize/MongoDB, not external APIs). LLM tools (searchProducts, getOrderById) call internal services. While /rest/country-mapping or /rest/track-order/:id may consume external APIs, architecture does not confirm outbound integrations — only potential endpoints. Insufficient evidence to confirm unsafe consumption.

name: LLM01: Prompt Injection
evidence: Genuine tool-calling LLM system detected: four tools (searchProducts, getProductReviews, getOrderById, generateCoupon) are defined with Zod schemas and execute real side-effects. System prompt enforces tool usage (e.g., 'MUST use searchProducts whenever...'). This creates a direct prompt injection surface — malicious user input can manipulate tool selection or arguments — satisfying structural prerequisite.

name: LLM02: Sensitive Information Disclosure
evidence: LLM tools execute database queries (Sequelize + MongoDB) and return raw results (e.g., getProductReviews, getOrderById). Tool schemas and execution logic are exposed in source (routes/*.ts), and no output filtering or PII redaction is indicated. Combined with frontend escape hatches (28 bypassSecurityTrustHtml instances), LLM output could be injected into DOM — creating disclosure risk. Structural prerequisite (LLM returning sensitive data without sanitization) is present.

name: LLM03: Supply Chain
evidence: No LLM-related supply chain components detected: no model weights, no Hugging Face/Transformers dependencies, no ONNX/Triton artifacts, no remote model hosting. LLM functionality is entirely built on @ai-sdk/openai-compatible (a lightweight SDK) and local tool functions — no external model binaries or pipelines. Architecture lacks any LLM model distribution or inference supply chain.

name: LLM05: Improper Output Handling
evidence: Frontend uses 28 Angular innerHTML/bypassSecurityTrustHtml escape hatches — many in LLM-adjacent contexts (chatbot, search-result, feedback-details, track-result). LLM output is streamed and rendered unsafely, enabling XSS if tool responses contain HTML/script. This is improper output handling: LLM-generated content is inserted into DOM without sanitization — structural prerequisite confirmed.

name: LLM06: Excessive Agency
evidence: LLM tools perform high-privilege actions: generateCoupon (financial impact), getOrderById (accesses order history), and searchProducts (may trigger expensive DB scans). System prompt grants broad authority ('MUST use...'), and no runtime agency limiting (e.g., max tool calls, cost caps, approval gates) is evident in route or tool definitions. Structural prerequisite — LLM authorized to perform impactful actions — is satisfied.

name: LLM10: Unbounded Consumption
evidence: No rate limiting, token budgeting, or timeout controls visible on LLM endpoints (/rest/chat, /rest/web3/*). Tools like searchProducts and getProductReviews lack query limits or pagination enforcement in route definitions. Combined with unrestricted /metrics and /rest/basket/:id/checkout (auth: null), resource exhaustion via LLM-driven tool invocation is structurally possible.
